fields.title: Who calls whom
fields.keyTakeaway: A webhook gives speed, polling gives control, and reliable integration usually uses both: a webhook for speed and periodic reconciliation for a guarantee.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: A partner updated an order status. Do we find out in a second or in five minutes — and what does that depend on?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Recognition delay turns directly into product quality: how up-to-date statuses are, how fast notifications arrive, whether the app displays yesterday's price. The choice of mechanism determines this delay and is made once during integration.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: **[[polling-2|Polling]].** We regularly ask "what's new". Simple, fully under our control, works with any API. The price is delay up to the polling interval and many empty requests. With a minute interval and a thousand objects, this is noticeable load for rare changes.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[webhook|Webhook]].** The external system calls us directly when an event occurs. Delay in seconds, no extra requests. The price is complexity: you need a public address, you must accept load at the exact moment someone else decides to create it, and you must decide what to do if you were unavailable at that moment.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **[[long-polling|Long polling]].** A compromise: the request hangs until news appears. Delay almost like a webhook, infrastructure almost like polling.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: Four questions that determine the choice:
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *How fast do you need to know?* Delivery status — minutes are acceptable. Payment confirmation — seconds. *How often do events happen?* Rare events with frequent polling is a waste of resources. *Does the provider have webhooks?* Often the question ends here. *What if we were unavailable?* A webhook might not retry. You need either a retry on their side or periodic reconciliation.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: The last point is the main practical advice: **webhooks are almost always supplemented by periodic reconciliation.** A webhook gives speed, reconciliation gives a guarantee. Webhooks alone mean that every minute of our downtime turns into lost events.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Separately — **[[webhook-signature|webhook signature]].** An incoming webhook is a request from the internet that anyone can send. Without signature verification, anyone can tell us that an order is paid.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: *Payment provider* — webhooks plus reconciliation. The webhook confirms payment in seconds. Every five minutes we reconcile payments in "pending" status with their API. Reconciliation catches 3–5 cases a day where the webhook did not arrive.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Delivery service* — webhooks for status changes, reconciliation every 15 minutes for active orders.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Catalog suppliers* — no webhooks, polling once an hour, limited by their rate limits. The product consequence regarding price freshness was covered in block `IN1`.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: The incident that shaped this practice: during a new version rollout, the service accepted webhooks with errors for forty minutes. The provider retries three times over ten minutes, then gives up. We lost 60 payment confirmations — people paid, orders hung as unpaid. Reconciliation, introduced after this, cost two days of work and has closed such cases automatically ever since.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Webhooks create load we do not control: a provider can send a thousand events at once after their own outage. Accepting a webhook must be fast — put it in a queue and respond, rather than processing it synchronously.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A webhook gives speed, polling gives control, and reliable integration usually uses both: a webhook for speed and periodic reconciliation for a guarantee.
